component.name: Dish
component.summary: Stream a gamepad to a Satellite server over your LAN

description.p: Dish turns this machine into a wireless gamepad for a Satellite server on the same network. Pair once, pick a controller, and the pad's sticks, buttons, motion and rumble travel over an encrypted UDP channel.
Dish can:

ul.li: Find Satellite servers on the LAN automatically, or connect by address
Pair with trust-on-first-use key pinning, so a swapped server is caught
Stream up to four pads at once, each mapped to its own remote slot
Carry rumble, battery level, motion and touchpad input both ways
Remap buttons, tune deadzones, and save a layout per controller
Claim supported pads directly over USB, for a higher polling rate

description.p: Dish never installs its own updates. It can check for a new release and link out to it, and your package manager owns the binary. In the Flatpak that check starts off, because Flathub delivers the updates.

Dish also checks dish.tinkernorth.com for a newer list of the controllers it recognises, shortly after launch and every six hours. The request carries no identifier, and a switch in Settings turns it off.

screenshot.caption: A connected pad, ready to bind to a satellite
Connected controllers and what each one supports
Theme, forwarded features and controller tuning

description.p: Dish ships the controller list the whole Dish family now shares, 272 controllers, and checks dish.tinkernorth.com for a newer one ten seconds after it starts and every six hours, with no identifier; Settings turns the check off, and with it off nothing is asked. Each controller's Diagnostics card names the record it matched, whether that record is verified, any known issue for this computer, what the controller's descriptor showed against the record, and the last report Dish wrote to it.

The controller inspector tests every output a controller's connection carries (rumble, trigger rumble, light bar, player lights, adaptive triggers, mic lamp, speaker tone, haptics and microphone level) and its sticks, puts back what the game had set, and asks "Did it work?" after each test.

Report a problem and Ask a question save a file of what the Diagnostics page shows, with your words in it, and open your own mail app addressed to support@tinkernorth.com; the file's folder opens too, in case your mail app leaves the file out. Nothing is sent until you press Send, and the file never holds pairing keys, addresses or the names of your hosts. A report can capture the controller it is about: its USB descriptors and twenty reports taken while it lies still.

A controller the list names, and Dish's own tables do not, now decodes on the Direct path by its record's family, and a verified one goes Direct by itself; a newer list applies to a controller the next time it is plugged in.

A controller's microphone, speaker and haptics are promised to the satellite only when this computer will carry them. Dish told the satellite it would play a DualSense's haptics as audio whenever the controller's sound output had four channels and its speaker switch was on, but it opened the voice only once the satellite had also said it carries that direction, and never for an output the audio stack refused to open; the satellite trusted the promise and sent the haptics as audio instead of turning them into rumble, so a game's haptics went silent. The promise now follows the same rule as the voices, an output Dish cannot open is not asked for again until the controller is plugged in again or the output changes, and the satellite turns the haptics into rumble meanwhile.

Dish speaks Satellite protocol 4, so a controller's extra buttons (back paddles, a Steam Controller's "..." button, trackpad and trigger clicks, stick and grip touches) reach the host from Steam Controllers, a DualSense Edge, a Switch Pro Controller and controllers read through SDL, and a Satellite can ask for a DualSense Edge. A Steam Controller's card picks what its trackpads are: right stick, touchpad or off. The 2026 Steam Controller can be taken over on USB direct, every controller on a Steam Controller receiver reads as a pad of its own, and two identical controllers on USB direct each get a card of their own. A host is sent the lower of the controller's battery and the computer's, which the privacy policy now names, DualSense rumble on USB direct asks the pad the way its own driver does, and the controller inspector shows the extra buttons. The Steam Controller and DualSense Edge buttons, the receiver and two identical controllers on USB direct have not been tried on real hardware yet.

Controller input leaves on its own thread without waiting on any lock: a plugged-in pad is read every half millisecond, each change goes out once, rumble and lights never hold up the next message from Satellite, and the input, USB, network and microphone threads ask for a higher priority through rtkit or the realtime portal. Every release now carries a measurement of the input path.

Dish can keep a laptop streaming with the lid closed: a new switch in Settings, Power, off by default, holds the lid switch while Dish is keeping the computer awake. The pairing sheet takes the satellite's four-digit PIN, so a typed PIN can be submitted again.

A Direct controller that re-enumerates comes back instead of going quiet, and one that reads nothing falls back to Standard. 8BitDo pads in D-input mode and the PlayStation Classic controller decode in their own button orders. The Guide button reaches the host from the Standard path. The setup wizard no longer pre-selects a Steam Deck's own controls, diagnostics shows each controller's USB ID, and the AppImage says SteamOS needs no udev rule.

A stick pushed all the way up no longer reads as all the way down, whatever the pad. A Moonlight host now gets the touchpad click and the Guide button, and the light bar's Off setting covers it too. The emulated Xbox and Nintendo pads carry trigger rumble and a battery. Controller audio is steadier: the microphone keeps its count across a reopen, the speaker's queue stays short after a stall, a restarted stream plays again, and an unplugged and replugged audio device reopens.

The dish on the launcher icon, in the tray and in the window faces its signal: the reflector aimed up and to the left while the signal arcs sat at the upper right, and it now points at them in every state glyph and in the app mark.

The AppImage no longer crashes on a dialog's Cancel button (Qt 6.10.3), and the Flatpak reports crashes like every other package. A Diagnostics page shows each session and each controller down to the wire. A controller goes back on its Moonlight host after a restart and the binding follows the pad, not the order pads were plugged. The Rumble switch and the touchpad's Pad choice work, a satellite you disconnect stays disconnected, and a reinstalled satellite says so.

Protocol 3: a DualSense's HD haptics reach the pad over Satellite, and adaptive triggers, player LEDs and the mic lamp now work on the Standard path too. Bluetooth Sony pads attach with everything SDL can drive, a Direct-claimed pad shows its own battery, controller audio works on the Standard path, and every host row carries the link-tier, protocol and microphone cues Dish for Android has.

One version number across Dish and Satellite. Adds the controller microphone and speaker over the Satellite protocol, Moonlight hosts (Sunshine, Apollo, Wolf), controller lights and adaptive triggers that follow the game, and crash reports that are actually sent, behind the same opt-out switch every other Dish client has.
Adds version-less stable download names for every package, so the newest build is always available at the same link. No changes to the client itself.

Fixes the tray icon showing as a missing-icon placeholder when Dish's launcher icons are not installed in the icon theme, as with the AppImage or a source build: the tray now ships the brand mark inside the client and advertises a theme icon name only where the theme can resolve it.
Fixes the AppImage on Wayland desktops: the bundle now carries Qt's client buffer integrations, without which 0.1.1's predecessor aborted at startup outside X11.
First Linux release: Qt Quick UI, LAN and mDNS discovery, TOFU pairing, SDL and USB-direct input paths, and six UI languages.
